definition.text: In-situ conservation protects species and their genetic resources on site, in the natural populations where they live.

facts.text: Its opposite is ex situ conservation, where threatened species or their material are kept elsewhere, as in seed libraries and gene banks.
Methods include nature reserves, national parks, wildlife sanctuaries, biodiversity hotspots and gene sanctuaries.
It keeps populations in the setting where they developed their traits and lets evolution and adaptation carry on.
Reserves must be large enough to hold populations with the genetic diversity needed to keep adapting.
Ex situ conservation is a last resort when in situ conservation is too difficult or impossible.

definition.text: A biosphere reserve is a protected area designed to serve both biodiversity conservation and sustainable development.

facts.text: The concept dates from the 1970s and uses core, buffer and transition zones to balance conservation with development.
By 2004 about 459 such areas had been set up in 97 countries.
A gene sanctuary, where plants are conserved, includes both biosphere reserves and national parks.

definition.text: On-farm conservation keeps traditional crop varieties alive by improving them with farmers in their own fields.

facts.text: Gene-bank samples and farmers' seed of a variety are tested together, the best are crossed and multiplied, and the improved seed goes back to producers.
This lets farmers keep their own varieties instead of switching to commercial ones or abandoning the crop.
It works best in marginal areas where climate or soil rule out commercial varieties, or where taste makes up for lower yields.

title: Insular biogeography

definition.text: Island biogeography studies what controls the number and diversification of species in isolated natural communities.

facts.text: Robert MacArthur and E. O. Wilson started the field in the 1960s.
Its theory holds that an island's species number is set by a balance between immigration and extinction.
Remote islands receive fewer immigrants, while larger islands have more habitat and lower chance-driven extinction.
An 'island' can be any patch of suitable habitat surrounded by unsuitable land, such as a mountaintop, a woodland or a national park amid development.
Simberloff and Wilson cleared arthropods from small Florida mangrove islands; within a year they were recolonized, nearer islands fastest.
Seeing reserves as habitat islands raised fears they would lose species, and led to the SLOSS debate and to wildlife corridors.

contested_note: Ecologists vigorously debated its use in reserve design, notably whether one large reserve beats several small ones.

definition.text: The species–area relationship describes how the number of species found grows with the size of the habitat area sampled.

facts.text: It is often written as the power law S = cA^z, where S is species number, A is area and z the slope.
On log–log axes it becomes a straight line: log(S) = log(c) + z log(A).
Conservation science uses it to predict extinction rates from habitat loss and fragmentation.
Larger islands usually have more species, but a smaller island can sometimes hold more than a larger one.

definition.text: Key Biodiversity Areas are places judged internationally important for biodiversity under global criteria published by the IUCN.

facts.text: They identify areas that governments or other agencies need to protect, extending the Important Bird Area idea to other groups.
Sites qualify on vulnerability and irreplaceability; the global standard was published in 2016.
The standard covers over 16,000 areas totalling 21,000,000 km2.
Critics say the criteria may be too broad: one analysis found 26% to 68% of Earth's land could qualify.

definition.text: Biodiversity is measured with objective indicators, most often the number of taxa found in an area over a period of time.

facts.text: Species richness, species evenness and species diversity are worked out first; diversity combines richness and evenness.
The Shannon and Simpson diversity indices are the two most popular measures.
Diversity can be measured at different scales: alpha within a site, beta between sites and gamma across a region.
Each measure suits a particular use of the data; a more economically defensible one would preserve options for adaptation and future human use.
Since it is unclear which genes may prove useful, keeping as many genes as possible is the best choice for conservation.

definition.text: The Biodiversity Intactness Index measures change in biodiversity using worldwide abundance data on plants, fungi and animals.

facts.text: It shows how local land biodiversity responds to pressures such as land-use change and intensification.
The related Mean Species Abundance Index tracks population trends across a cross-section of species.

title: Phylogenetic and functional diversity
article: Measurement of biodiversity#Other measures of diversity

definition.text: Phylogenetic and functional diversity measures add information on how species are related and on their functional traits, not just their number.

facts.text: Examples include Faith's 1992 phylogenetic diversity index and functional group richness.
Different kinds of diversity are not necessarily independent; vertebrate taxonomic and ecological diversity are closely linked.
